rv.q: We could have done with fewer clichés: When a drug dealer says, “After tonight, I’m out of the game for good,” you just know things won’t end well.
Despite a clunky book, this show is on fire.
The high-energy, deeply felt but ultimately overwrought production
In the end, "Holler" leaves you feeling more exhausted than inspired.
And so while I admire Holler If Ya Hear Me’s attempt to add its new voice to the medium, there’s only so much rage it can take.
But Holler is a shapeless mix of melodrama, music video and half-grasped musical clichés.

Unfortunately, much else about this ambitious show, which opened on Thursday at the Palace Theater, feels heartfelt but heavy-handed, as it punches home its message with a relentlessness that may soon leave you numb to the tragic story it’s trying to tell.
While it might be remembered as the first Broadway musical to use the N-word as punctuation (as well as the M.F. one), this otherwise looks likely to be forgotten fast.
After the first hour, it’s strictly all eyez on the exit.
This is way more than most Broadway shows ever provide, and could serve as a template for the future.
By celebrating its subject's creativity rather than exploiting his legend, Holler sets a fundamentally positive example for a problematic form.
Holler If Ya Hear Me is at its most thrilling during these moments when the star connects with the audience through spoken word poetry that channels anger into art.

But the two-dozen songs lushly presented in the $8 million production directed by Kenny Leon (who just nabbed a Tony for “A Raisin in the Sun”) are threaded together by a fictional story so tired, and so often told, that you can’t help but walk away feeling that an opportunity has been missed.
The production is vibrant, raw and rousing, but it self-sabotages with predictability and unintelligibility.
The effect of the repackaging is to affirm Shakur's artistry without demonstrating that it works particularly well in musical theater.
The whole thing makes you want to holler.
Holler If Ya Hear Me doesn't, alas, offer nearly half as much worth hearing.
Otherwise, this show keeps falling prey to almost every cliché that has made the jukebox musical such a maligned genre in the theater.
Too bad this Holler is more like a shout we’ve heard before.
So it’s extremely disheartening to report that “Holler If Ya Hear Me” is a total mess and misfire.

cn.t: Tupac's music energizes this ambitious Broadway rap musical, but critics find it hampered by a generic, heavy-handed book. Performances and production values earn praise, yet the show struggles to match its groundbreaking sound with compelling storytelling.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.
